newsitem.title: USA: Kindercare to merge with unit of KKR.
newsitem.headline: Kindercare to merge with unit of KKR.

text.p: Kindercare Learning Centres Inc. said Thursday it agreed to merge with an affiliate of Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co., the New York-based investment group, in a deal worth $600 million.
Kindercare, the nation's largest chain of preschool and child care centres, said the merger would give it the financial flexibility it needed to further expand.

The company, with 1,148 child centres in 38 states and Britain, has grown rapidly as more women have found jobs, fuelling demand for outside child care. It had about 120,000 full-time and part-time children enrolled in its programmes as of May 1996.

The investment company Oaktree Capital Management and affiliates who own 52 percent of Kindercare stock have agreed to vote their shares in favour of the merger, in which shareholders can choose to receive either $20.25 in cash per share or retain existing Kindercare stock, the company said.
After the merger, a Kohlberg Kravis Roberts (KKR) affiliate will own 85 percent of Kindercare and other shareholders will own the rest of the Montgomery, Ala.-based company.
The total value of the deal, including equity and debt, is about $600 million, the company said in a statement.
Kindercare has also won a commitment from Chase Manhattan Corp., which is financing the deal along with Kindercare and KKR, for $300 million in debt to fund expansion and acquisitions.

"Our new capital structure is conservative, flexible, and designed to fund expansion, continue innovation, and further our commitment to the highest standards of cost effective, quality preschool and child care," Kindercare Chairman Sandra Scarr said.
After the merger, Kindercare will be capitalised with $175 million of equity, of which $148.75 million will be invested by a KKR affiliate.

Traders bid $19 for Kindercare stock in after-hours action, up $3 from $16 at the close of regular trading, but the stock was not actually trading after Nasdaq ordered a halt to dealing, traders said.
